summary: Analyzes how enterprise networks, which have multiple internal links and connections to one or more providers, can move to IPv6, focusing on the IP layer. It identifies transition scenarios and requirements that build on an earlier document about enterprise scenarios. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo is a plan for moving a company network to IPv6. It assumes both protocols will run side by side for a while, and it works at the level of addresses, routing and the links between sites. It ends with advice on which tool to use where the two worlds meet.

questions: how do enterprises transition to ipv6
how do enterprises move to ipv6
what is the ipv6 enterprise scenario matrix
subtitle: A plan for moving an organisation's network to IPv6 while running both protocols side by side.

tldr.problem: An enterprise network has several internal links, one or more provider connections and a mix of applications, and nobody had written down which combinations of IPv4 and IPv6 they would actually meet, or what to do about each.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC builds a matrix of ten notional networks, analyses three deployment strategies (wide-scale dual-stack, sparse dual-stack and IPv6-dominant), lays out a three-stage plan for the basic services, and then says which transition mechanism belongs at each incompatible network touchpoint.
tldr.outcome: The document is analysis rather than specification. It is informational, has not been obsoleted, and it points at the enterprise scenarios document RFC 4057 for the cases it expands on.

today: RFC 4852 is an Informational document published in April 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is analysis rather than specification, and it expands on the enterprise scenarios in RFC 4057. Its recommendations, such as the /48 site allocation and the /64 subnet size, describe the practice it observed at the time.

sections.title: Purpose, Scope and Vocabulary
sections.content:
The RFC analyses how an enterprise network moves to IPv6, looking only at IP layer 3. The networks it describes have several internal links and one or more router connections to one or more providers, and they are run by a network operations team. The analysis works from a set of notional networks and requirements expanded from an earlier document on enterprise scenarios, and it assumes a dual-IP layer environment, meaning IPv4 and IPv6 both exist across the enterprise's network and hosts. It then recommends a transition mechanism for each notional network.

The audience is the enterprise network team planning an IPv6 deployment, and the document is aimed at teams from management, network operations and engineering. The analysis and the notional networks are an example set of cases an enterprise can use to build its own transition strategy.

Several topics are deliberately out of scope: multihoming, application porting, IPv6 VPN, firewall or intrusion detection deployment, IPv6 network management and QoS, novel IPv6 services such as Mobile IPv6, requirements at the provider's network, and IPv6-only future deployment scenarios. The document also says nothing about network address translation or provider independent address space. It covers IPv6 on the wire, including address management and DNS services, and assumes the deployment is run by the network administration team rather than by an individual user gaining IPv6 connectivity from inside the enterprise network.

The vocabulary is precise. An enterprise network has multiple internal links, one or more router connections to one or more providers, and is actively managed by a network operations entity. A provider supplies services and connectivity to the Internet or to other private external networks. A node or network is IPv6-capable if it can support both IPv6 and IPv4, IPv4-only if it supports only IPv4, and IPv6-only if it supports only IPv6, which does not imply an IPv6-only stack. Dual-IP means a network or node supporting both. The IP-capability of a node is its ability to support IPv6 only, IPv4 only, or both. A network is IPv6-dominant when it runs IPv6 routing and control plane services and provides transport for both IPv4 and IPv6 protocol services. A transition implementation is the network strategy the enterprise uses to move to IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a plan for moving a company network to IPv6. It assumes both protocols will run side by side for a while, and it works at the level of addresses, routing and the links between sites. It is careful about its words: dual-IP means both protocols, IPv6-dominant means IPv6 routing carries even the old IPv4 traffic, and a transition implementation is simply the plan for getting there.

sections.title: The Enterprise Scenario Matrix
sections.content:
The analysis starts from a matrix of ten notional networks, called scenarios A to J, each row describing one situation an enterprise may meet. The first column gives the protocol used by the application and, below it, the IP-capability of the node sending the packets. The second column gives the IP-capability of the network the node is attached to. The third gives the IP-capability of the service provider's network. The fourth gives the IP-capability of the destination network, and the fifth gives the protocol used by the application and the IP-capability of the receiving node.

The notional enterprise has hosts attached to enterprise-owned intranets at two different global locations separated by the Internet. The enterprise owns and runs its own intranets but relies on an external provider for Internet service. Both intranets are run by different organisations inside the same enterprise, so they can sit at different points in the transition at the same time. Trivial cases such as pure IPv4, pure IPv6 and ubiquitous dual-IP are left out, and the authors say they could not conceive of IPv6-only providers or IPv6-only nodes in the near term, so those cases are not covered either. They assume all nodes hosting IPv6 applications are dual-IP, and they recommend that network address translation not be used in these notional cases.

Scenarios A to C are variations of compatible hosts talking across largely homogeneous networks, where the packet must cross at least one incompatible network component. Scenario B is an enterprise that wants IPv6 applications but has not transitioned its internal networks and whose provider offers only IPv4. Scenario C is an enterprise that has transitioned its core networks, as has its provider, but which still runs a legacy IPv4 application. Scenario D is the unusual case where the core intranets have moved to IPv6 but the provider has not, and critical legacy IPv4 applications must still work across the mixed environment. Scenarios E to J are the harder cases: the enterprise has both IPv4 and IPv6 versions of the same application that must interoperate, with a variety of mixed segments between them. Scenario E is an enterprise that has largely transitioned but still has a few legacy IPv4 applications. Scenario J is the opposite extreme, where IPv6 applications and network segments are rare.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo sorts the possible situations into ten rows, from easy to awkward. Each row asks five questions: what does the sending application use, what can its network carry, what can the provider carry, what can the receiving network carry, and what does the receiving application use. The awkward rows are the ones where the answers disagree.

sections.title: Wide-Scale Dual-Stack Deployment
sections.content:
In the wide-scale case the administrator introduces IPv6 on the wire inside the existing IPv4 infrastructure in a structured way, so that a number of IPv4 routers, and with them their subnets, become dual-IP. The reason may not be immediate wide-scale use of IPv6 but rather to prepare the infrastructure for IPv6-capable nodes, so that IPv6 can be turned on on demand. The deployment should be staged, with IPv6 enabled on specific links at various stages, some links staying IPv4-only and some deliberately left without IPv6 connectivity. A typical deployment starts with a single testbed dual-IP subnet at the site, which lets the IPv6 capability of specific platforms and applications be evaluated and verified without risking the production network.

The critical choice is the routing infrastructure. Where IPv6 routing capability already exists in the infrastructure, the administrator can enable IPv6 on the same physical hardware as the existing IPv4 service, which is the end goal once the capability, performance and robustness of dual-IP operation have been verified. Ideally the IPv6 capability spans the entire enterprise, so it can be deployed on any link or subnet.

Where the enterprise cannot provide IPv6 routing at first, there are two choices. It can tunnel IPv6 over some or all of the existing IPv4 infrastructure, establishing tunnels between the dual-IP capable routers so that routers and platforms which are not IPv6-capable are bypassed. Or it can deploy a parallel IPv6 routing infrastructure, with new IPv6-capable routers providing IPv6 connectivity into existing IPv4 subnets, either over dedicated physical links or, where available, over IEEE 802.1q VLANs, which need no extra cabling and let several IPv6 links share one physical interface. The parallel approach probably needs additional hardware, but it leaves the existing IPv4 routing platforms undisturbed, and the RFC says it should be seen only as an interim step towards full dual-IP on a unified infrastructure. When the enterprise's users are off-site and their ISP offers neither native IPv6 nor transition help, the enterprise may deploy its own remote IPv6 access, for example with an IPv6 Tunnel Broker.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the big rollout: turn IPv6 on across the existing network rather than adding a second network alongside it. Where the routers can already do IPv6, switch it on. Where they cannot, either tunnel IPv6 through the old IPv4 routers or build a separate IPv6 network that reaches into the old subnets, and treat that separate network as temporary.

sections.title: Sparse and IPv6-Dominant Deployment
sections.content:
Sparse deployment suits an enterprise that needs IPv6 for a few mission-critical applications or services. Only the nodes running those applications are upgraded to be IPv6-capable; the routing infrastructure is not upgraded, and the enterprise does not want a parallel IPv6 routing infrastructure yet, since that option was already covered. End-to-end IPv6 communication is needed but the infrastructure only supports IPv4 routing, so the only viable method is to tunnel the traffic over the existing IPv4 infrastructure. The network team must pick the most efficient mechanism to deploy so that the existing IPv4 infrastructure is not disrupted, and two questions follow. The first is where the tunnel endpoint sits: using the provider's own transition service means individual nodes need their own IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnel and all IPv6 traffic must be forwarded by the enterprise's IPv4 infrastructure to that endpoint, which is somewhat inefficient but acceptable when the applications need no intranetwork communication at all. Alternatively the enterprise can deploy its own transition node, possibly collocated next to the border router that connects to the provider, which also allows intranetwork traffic to use the tunnel. The second question is manual or automatic: with few nodes, statically configured tunnels will do, while with more nodes automatically configured tunnels may be preferable.

An IPv6-dominant network is one where IPv6 routing carries both IPv4 and IPv6 packets, even though the network is dual-IP capable, and IPv4 routing is not turned on except where edge IPv4 networks require it. Communication between IPv6 nodes uses IPv6. When an IPv6-capable node in such a network has to reach an IPv4 node, it uses its dual-IP implementation to tunnel IPv4 inside IPv6, and an edge router in the IPv6-dominant network decapsulates the IPv4 packet and routes it to the IPv4 node. In each case a transition point has to exist inside the network, the node must acquire an IPv4 address, and it must locate a tunnel endpoint that can carry the IPv4 packet to the next-hop IPv6 router and on to a destination dual-IP router. The RFC warns that maintaining IPv4 services in an IPv6-dominant network slows, and may even impede, the ability to gain the maximum benefits of IPv6. Whether to use this strategy is driven entirely by the enterprise's business and operational objectives and guided by its transition plan.
sections.plainLanguage: Two other shapes are possible. In the sparse one, only the few machines that need IPv6 are upgraded and everything else is tunnelled through the old IPv4 network. In the IPv6-dominant one, IPv6 routing carries everything, and the old IPv4 traffic is tunnelled inside IPv6 instead. The memo warns that keeping IPv4 alive this way holds back the gains from IPv6.

sections.title: The Staged Deployment Plan
sections.content:
Whatever the strategy, the administrator needs a staged plan, starting with a strategic identification of every point and component of the transition. Stage one is about connectivity rather than technical detail: select an external IPv6 provider, typically a topographically close one able to provide an IPv6 upstream link, and obtain globally routable IPv6 address space from it as provider-assigned address space. The RFC says the enterprise should receive at least a /48 allocation, and it points to a separate document for renumbering if the provider changes. Native IPv6 upstream connectivity is expected, or a manually configured tunnel where that is not available.

Stage two deploys the basic service components. Each site needs an IPv6 addressing plan built on the globally aggregatable public prefix the provider allocated. IPv6 links may be made congruent with the existing IPv4 subnets, and prefix allocations should leave room for topological growth so that restructuring does not force renumbering. IPv6 saves address conservation effort: a site running IPv4 allocates subnets as small as possible, for example a /26 for 50 nodes, which then needs larger prefixes and disruptive renumbering as the subnet grows, while an IPv6 link can in effect have any number of nodes. Best practice at the time of writing was restricted by the small number of wide-scale deployments, so the advice is to allocate /64 size prefixes for subnets and reserve space for growth. The site should also run a DNS service that serves IPv6 records in the AAAA format and can communicate over IPv6 transport, and it needs IPv6 routing inside and out: a static route to a single upstream provider may be enough for a single-homed site, while an interior routing protocol such as BGP4+, IS-IS, OSPFv3 or RIPng can be used internally.

Host configuration follows the IPv4 pattern. Manual configuration, NIS and DHCPv4 are the IPv4 tools; for IPv6, Stateless Address Autoconfiguration can give a host a global address, a default router and on-link prefix information, with SEND available where secure autoconfiguration is required. A stateless node that wants other settings, such as DNS or NTP servers, will need a stateful DHCPv6 service, and a DHCPv6 Relay Agent function where the DHCPv6 servers are off-link. Hosts may also generate or request IPv6 Privacy Addresses.

Security has to be applied to IPv6 exactly as it is to IPv4. The border firewall should filter and control IPv6 traffic by enforcing the same policy it already does for IPv4. The site's security policy must be reviewed in light of the IPv6-specific functionality being deployed, such as Mobile IPv6, stateless autoconfiguration and SEND, IPv6 privacy extensions and end-to-end IPsec, and for the use of globally aggregatable public address space where private addressing and NAT had been used. Intrusion detection systems need to be enhanced to check IPv6 transport, both for known application layer attack patterns and for new IPv6 threats such as excessive hop-by-hop headers or errant IPv6 header options. Transition mechanisms can introduce threats of their own, such as carrying IPv6 data tunnelled in IPv4, so the site security policy should cover the mechanisms actually deployed. Stage three then rolls the IPv6 capability out to the wider enterprise: turning IPv6 on the wire in the desired links and enabling applications and other services to begin using IPv6 transport.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan comes in three stages. First get connected and get real address space, at least a /48. Then build the basics: an addressing plan, DNS that speaks IPv6, IPv6 routing, and a way to configure hosts. Only then turn IPv6 on across the site. Security is not a separate stage; the same policy as IPv4 has to cover the new protocol, the new mechanisms and the new traffic.

sections.title: Choosing Transition Mechanisms
sections.content:
The last part of the analysis is about picking mechanisms. Mapping a situation onto one of the ten scenarios matters less than spotting the touchpoints where incompatible networks meet, because that is where a mechanism has to go unless the enterprise offers it as a service. The ten scenarios boil down to four themes. The simplest and most favoured is widespread dual-IP with compatible hosts at either end. The second is compatible hosts with incompatible network segments in between, where tunnelling bypasses the incompatible segments: manually configured tunnels do the job but provide no automated tunnel configuration, and 6to4 can support enterprises that have no assigned IPv6 prefix address. Which device performs the tunnelling follows from where the incompatible touchpoint sits: if a local network is incompatible, host tunnelling is appropriate, and if the backbone or provider network is incompatible, gateway-to-gateway tunnelling may be better. Keeping tunnel endpoints at dual-IP devices preserves end-to-end communication.

Having IPv6 applications on a dual-IP host on an IPv4-only network also needs some form of tunnelling. Where configured tunnels are not enough, a more automatic solution may suit: ISATAP gives end-node IPv6 connectivity from nodes on an isolated IPv4 network, and Teredo works when the enterprise network is behind a NAT. Enterprise architects may also provide a Tunnel Broker as a cost-effective service to local users or applications, which can automate the use of tunnels across an enterprise deploying IPv6. Later in the transition, after the enterprise has largely moved to an IPv6 infrastructure, the architect needs a strategy for tunnelling IPv4 within IPv6 across IPv6-dominant links or the enterprise intranet.

The third theme is incompatible applications talking across a homogeneous network. Translation is the obvious solution, but the RFC does not recommend it except for legacy devices at the network edge that cannot or never will be upgraded to IPv6. A more scalable solution is an Application Layer Gateway between the incompatible hosts. The fourth theme mixes incompatible hosts and incompatible networks at the same time, which may need multiple, or even nested, transition mechanisms; for example an Application Layer Gateway collocated with the application server may be needed to service both IPv4 and IPv6 data streams that are simultaneously tunnelled through incompatible network segments. Section 9 points back to the security discussion in the staged plan, with the IPv6 transition and co-existence security considerations document as the detailed reference.
sections.plainLanguage: When choosing a tool, the memo says do not start from the scenario table. Find the places where two incompatible networks meet and put the tool there. Tunnels are for the network, an application gateway is for the applications, and sometimes you need both at once.
